comments.author: Kindly-Sail6260
comments.body:
Idk why that guy dm’d you, but it’s really just lighting. If you want realistic light, either go with actual raytracing or bake in lighting with global illumination and shadow maps to give some effect to them. You can also work on your post processing as well. Color grading isn’t usually enough on its own but it does help. I can’t help you fine tune the details, but usually those small tips are enough to help you in the long run once you get comfortable in knowing what you want.

Since you’re using AI, I’d ask your agent to a test on an empty map with RT or Baked lighting with GI enabled on both. You can get some really nice effects that’s way. 

Edit: you should also add intentional lighting sources in some areas to help as well as settings in exposure. Going deeper would require color grading in the shadows, midtones and highlights but that’s pretty advanced but maybe AI can swing it for your look

comments.author: Harrison_
comments.body:
Hey, looks pretty cool! Thought this was BF2 for a second. 10+ year former DP/colorist here.  
  
One general thought looking at what you're describing is not really a color grade/post process thing but a lighting ratio thing. When I think about the contrast ratio between things like lights in homes, tracer fire, etc for a night scene, in real life, those things are going to be 10x or 100x as bright (locally) as bright moon. When the moonlight is relatively dimmer, then you have pockets of warm light from environmental stuff that feels like it is actually illuminating only parts of the map, which creates what I think is realistic and nice visual contrast of dark and light areas. 

This map actually looks close-ish to what you'd see if you set a camera on a long exposure on a full moon night in the snow, but, the town lighting, vehicle lights, fires, etc would all be VERY bright in comparison.

comments.author: cpteric
comments.body:
main issue i see is lighting and difference on model quality and how the models treat shadows. Ç  
Your night scene is extremely bright, and it casts sun-like hard shadows with very little dark corners.  I don't see enough ambient occlusion or dimness of the ambient. From a rts perspective, that is great because of, you know, seen what your troops are doing, but from a close view it makes it toy-y.

your tracks are not reacting to the terrain irregularities, the suspension should react per bogie/axle, and your track marks spawn from the center of your vehicle instead of from each track, and they are not sized to that vehicle's tracks.

They don't displace (fake displace, i mean)  snow in any direction.

there's an abusive amount of motion blur.

the tracer rounds don't seem to illuminate as they go,  and the impacts on you don't leave any scorhcing or tiny dents, even if low cal they'd still do that.

the video i will provide is not well recorded ( a bad camera with very high minimum aperture means that even at '4K', it's still grainy af), but it brings the point:  
[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F7WrUEpJAFQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F7WrUEpJAFQ)

this also shows it even on a cloudy day:  
[https://www.youtube.com/shorts/GNlaT9a24H8](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/GNlaT9a24H8)

ofcourse the formula for the ground reflection isn't easy.  i read somewhere something super simplified like this works 'good enough':  
(if you're using HLSL on unreal):

reflection = saturate(((BrightnessMultiplier \* (Caliber \* Caliber)) / ((DistanceToGround \* DistanceToGround) + SafetyOffset)) - MoonlightThreshold);

*SafetyOffset = a value to prevent divisions by 0 when the bullet is like 1cm from the ground.*

*moonlight threshold = ambient light cutoff.*

i also suggest some noise mask and a falloff distance so it isn't an even 360º illumination around the tracer.

if you want to keep a high visibility variant, i suggest keeping the current illumination with a shader that pretends to be a current-gen high end night vision view, like hwat one can see through a DTNVS/ENVG-B/etc gen 3+, and have another illumination system for cinematic first or third person experience.

It has a very distinctive blue hue and some newer ones add false color tint along autofocus or even silhouette detection:

https://i.redd.it/06dzyienyi2i1.jpeg
